Medals Before Children

By: Tarryn Crossman | Commission

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
Extract from Investigation 1 - words of the victim
Do you believe that the system will ultimately fail other girls as well?
Absolutely. If the same people stay. If the same people are on the panel, if the same people are participating in the Free State, if the very same people are in GSA, why would anything change now?

Fast forward to 2025. I get a call from Hayley Walker, the former safeguarding officer at Gymnastics South Africa. The same woman who once defended the organisation during our investigation — now ready to talk about a systemic cover-up inside the sport.

Summary:
Gymnastics SA: Medals Before Children
Last year, we exposed how Gymnastics South Africa (GSA) was covering up abuse within the sport, allegations the organisation vehemently denied. At the time, Hayley Walker, then head of safeguarding, defended GSA’s systems, insisting the organisation had learnt its lesson and that children were finally safe.
Less than a year later, Hayley has resigned, and now she’s ready to speak out. She reveals a culture of systemic abuse and intimidation. At the centre of this latest scandal is Louis Fourie, one of South Africa’s top Olympic coaches, who runs his high-performance gym at Tuks. More than ten gymnasts have come forward accusing him of physical and emotional abuse. Instead of investigating the claims, GSA allegedly moved to suppress them, protecting the coach rather than the athletes.
This is a hair-raising exposé of how a national sports body continues to put glory before children, ignoring its own safeguarding policies while young athletes suffer in silence.

Gymnast: I am in Grade 1 here. These are our Free State colors. He called me Jelly tots because I didn’t have breasts.

Anonymous (Subtitles): when I tried to quit Derek burnt my feet with a lighter.

Lourensa: Did you ever discuss this with anyone else?

Anonymous (Subtitles): yes, the club did know about it was done in front of a lot of people

Tarryn voice-over: In June last year, we met female gymnasts who’d spent their childhoods being silenced by the very adults meant to protect them. they were dismissed by the one organization responsible for holding their coaches to account, Gymnastics South Africa. So, they came to us. To be heard
gymnast: All I remember is that we were asleep, and he woke me up, and I had to sleep the whole night with his thing in my hand.
Tarryn voice-over: In our previous investigation, we confronted Gymnastics South Africa over what appeared to be a cover-up; an attempt to protect the federation’s reputation at the expense of these alleged abuse victims
Lourensa: You are the president of GSA. Yes. And stops with you. Does it not? Yet it does stop with me as president.
Donny Jurgen: It's difficult to get down to the level of every club, every school. Besides the 300 clubs, we have 428 schools. it's a mammoth task. we are doing as much as we can with minimal resources.
Tarryn voice-over: Within a week of this broadcast, GSA’s executive committee was replaced.
FADE TO BLACK
Tarryn voice-over: Then last month, I got a surprising voice note from Hayley Walker, GSA’s safeguarding officer in 2024.
Hayley Voice Note - I was wondering if you maybe like to chat, I have another case with them. I have subsequently stepped down with gymnastics south Africa, as there safeguarding officer
Hayley Walker: all along I discouraged – THE VICTIMS - from going to the media because it impacts the perceptions of the case. But at the end of the day, I feel the victims need to know that they've fought everything they can to get the justice The system hasn't given them. we can make sure that people actually know the extent of the manipulation that's gone on.
Tarryn voice-over: Hayley believes that GSA is trying to cover up an abuse case involving one of its Elite coaches
Tyde Cooper: I'm a high-performance gymnast. I'm part of the squad for South Africa. in senior Olympic level
Tarryn voice-over:18-year-old, Tyde cooper was one of the first gymnasts to speak out against, ex springbok and Olympic high performance coach Louis Fourie
Tyde Cooper: I've trained with him basically since I was about 10 till 18. It was an emotional war zone. When we were getting stuff right, he liked us when we weren't getting stuff right. He'd be screaming and shouting at you, telling you that you're not good enough. He'd say you useless, you're not worthy.
Tyde Cooper: He made it seem like his approval was the be all and end all. It was something you kind of craved.
Tarryn voice-over: The story behind the alleged abuse, unraveled after one mom spotted the warning signs, and began asking questions. We’re hiding her identity to protect her family
Anonymous: I realized how scared they were of Louis, which I found very strange.
They said that Louis is too connected. They were too scared to come forward because of the power that he had

Tarryn voice-over: Even the coaches, women who’d competed at the highest level, refused to speak publicly.

Anonymous: She said to me that the culture is It's very toxic. A lot is happening, and she can't be speaking about it. because she's very scared.
Tarryn voice-over: More and more victims came forward anonymously, all with the same story.

Hayley Walker: when I look at grooming in sport particularly, I look for the patterns of multiple victims saying the same kind of, of thing, even though they're at different times.
And so that, for me was When the story started coming together
Tarryn (Subtitles): Did he ever physically hurt you Tyde?
Tyde Cooper: He'll just walk up to you and bite you on your arms, anywhere actually. Arm, leg, neck. It became a normal thing. Biting, Or he just lick his. You in line up and you lick his finger and stick it in your ear. or twirling your ponytail. He always used to make it seem like he meant it as a joke. But that was never a joke because he knew how uncomfortable we all felt about it.
Tarryn (Subtitles): Why The biting. I don't understand. that such strange behavior?
Tyde Cooper: I think it was a form of control because he knew that we would do whatever he. We wanted him to finally see us and not scream and shout at us. And eventually it became normalized. That's just how he is.

Tarryn voice-over: Tyde wasn’t the only gymnast who reported being bitten by Coach Fourie. Audrey Mulligan — who now lives in the United States — was just ten years old when she trained under him.
Audrey Mulligan: he said, you know, and you have to land properly, You can't stop.. If you don't land correctly, I'm going to bite you. And he grabbed my arm, and it was around here, so it was close to my chest. It felt uncomfortable. But he grabbed my little arm and bit me where it left visible teeth marks. after he bit me, he bit other girls down the line, And then it fast forwarded. He came back to my end of the line and said, and if you land your vault, I'll kiss you. And so he kissed the visible bite marks down the line again. And were there other coaches in the room? It was a full gym. And no one said anything. I think because the adults around me didn't say anything, I thought that somehow it was okay. I never told my parents anything until my 17th birthday when I finally sat them down and I said, listen, this happened, and I've submitted my statement.

Tarryn voice-over: In the middle of last year ten gymnasts and coaches agreed to be part of a formal complaint laid with Gymnastics South Africa against Louis Fourie. As the safeguarding officer at the time, Hayley was tasked with investigating the allegations.
Hayley Walker: if I look at the definition of the children's act and abuse, biting, is clearly outlined there. Emotional abuse is the intentional breaking down over criticism the isolation, all of that, those are all defined clearly by the act as acts of abuse. and a lot of people go, but historically that's how things happened. We know better, we know better now and we've known better for the last 20 years, which is why I then recommended it go to a panel hearing, The panel requests that Mr. Faree be suspended from all gymnastics roles with immediate effect.
Tarryn (Subtitles): And GSA said,
Hayley Walker: No suspension.
Tarryn voice-over: GSA claimed, it had refused to suspend Coach Fourie, as it was the end of the gymnastics year — and that as a long-standing and highly rated member of the federation, he should first face a hearing before considering a suspension.
Tarryn voice-over: Most of the victims in Hayley’s initial report had asked to remain anonymous. Under GSA’s own policy, no one, not even the new president, Adele Hein, should be able to identify them
Hayley Walker: At one point, the President made contact with me to say she wants to speak to the victims. And I said, no. when the hearing was set and the information was then sent to Mr. Faree, it would appear that he then gave the names of the victims to the President, who then tried to reach out to the victims directly. Her kind of comment to me was, you know, I'd like to see if we can't mediate this and get them around the roundtable to have a Discussion with him and us it felt to me like she was trying to prevent the hearing.
Tarryn voice-over: After fighting for close to a year to get GSA to take action, to protect these victims and all gymnasts, Hayley was done.
Hayley Walker: I just said, I can't, I can't. Those victims were so gracious and for me asking them to trust the process and then to have confidence breached like that. I told GSA that I was stepping down,
Tarryn voice-over: The victims continued pressuring GSA to suspend Coach Fourie, escalating their complaints to the SA Sports Confederation and Olympic Committee — SASCOC — which in turn put pressure on GSA to suspend him immediately.

Anonymous: it took months and being persistent and reaching out to whoever I could to get these voices heard that he was only then suspended.

Tarryn voice-over: Coach Fourie’s hearing eventually began early this year, but by then, half the victims had dropped out. The process had dragged on too long, and many felt victimised by GSA,
Audrey: They're saying that our voices don't matter because they're choosing not to listen to them.
Tarryn voice-over: Audrey and Tyde agreed to continue.
Tyde Cooper: I cannot let any other girl go through what I went through. the culture that I think GSA is setting is that it's alright, you can abuse your gymnast and it's fine, you don't need consequences.
Hayley Walker: This is bigger than Louis –Farie.It was never an attack on an individual. It was making sure that this behaviour doesn't happen in these spaces. Accountability
Tarryn voice-over: Last month, an independent panel finally found Fourie guilty of serious misconduct and issued a recommended sanction. GSA refused to release that report. The victims’ lawyers then demanded disclosure. Citing it confidentiality policy, GSA again declined. We’ve since heard from a source that the panel recommended a lifetime ban for Coach Fourie. GSA rejected it.
Hayley Walker: They were trying to protect Louis Forie because he is well-loved and liked and, you know, he is a senior coach within the environment.
Tarryn voice-over: GSA’s executive committee, unanimously agreed to lift Fourie's suspension in January next year, on condition that he completes safe guarding training and four behavioral sessions.
Hayley Walker: Having worked on historical cases, it’s really a slap in the face of the victims/ It's the lightest sanction I have seen in a case of this nature in any federation with a guilty finding.
Tarryn voice-over: GSA president, Adele Hein, responded to our questions by requesting a live interview, which we couldn’t agree to. In a later written response she stood by GSA’s decision to lift Fourie’s suspension, saying GSA’s sanctions were fair, proportionate, and in line with its disciplinary framework.”
She went on to say that Safe Sport posters and educational materials are being distributed to all registered clubs … showing zero-tolerance to any form of abuse or misconduct.
Anonymous: Now he's even more powerful. because he's gotten away with it. he's, like, unstoppable.
Tarryn voice-over: When we first contacted Louis Fourie, he agreed to go on-camera.
Louis Fourie on the phone(Subtitles): I'll do an interview. I really don't mind. I do agree that I was, for certain actions, not appropriate, you know. Playing little games with the little eight-year-olds, which is generationally what we used to do. Because I think I owe it to my country's coaches. that a fair, transparent account of what actually materialized is given.
Tarryn Voice-over: But a few days later, we received a lawyer’s letter saying Louis could no longer speak to us as the disciplinary process had been confidential. The letter added that the coach was the victim of a “witch hunt” by disgruntled individuals intent on destroying his reputation.

Instead of investigating the claims, GSA allegedly moved to suppress them, protecting the coach rather than the athletes. This is a hair-raising exposé of how a national sports body continues to put glory before children, ignoring its own safeguarding policies while young athletes suffer in silence.
